newsitem.title: UK: Lead slumps to 8-1/2 month LME low, copper ends up.
newsitem.headline: Lead slumps to 8-1/2 month LME low, copper ends up.

text.p: Lead prices took a hammering during Friday LME trading, with a depressed market dropping to its lowest levels since end-January looking like falling further, traders said.
Other metals finished mixed with copper closing on a positive note after a large LME warehouse inventory fall, although the market baulked at $1,950 again.

Lead was pummelled lower during the afternoon rings and kerb, with the breach of $730 triggering speculative sell-stops down to a low of $715 before a last trade at $719, down $13. Despite being oversold, a test of $700 is likely, they said.

Traders said the upcoming battery season and expected better demand from the auto sector is as yet having little impact on a market grappling with negative sentiment. The indefinite suspension of operations at the Bougrine mine in Tunisia was ignored, as annual capacity is just 8,000 tonnes.
Also, stocks are rising and the Chinese are exporting more metal at present, analysts noted.

Copper prices fluctuated, unable to penetrate $1,950, but supported on dips which kept the market in the plus column. Underlying sentiment was helped by a large 19,125-tonne stock fall, although there are doubts over how much is actual offtake.
Copper is moving out of a wide range of geographical locations, and although some is going into consumption significant tonnages reflect arbitrage with New York and China.

Final kerb business was at $1,940, up $16 a tonne. Cash/threes finished at a slightly wider $32/34 backwardation, reflecting metal lent to the market in the summer now departing. Total LME inventory of 172,425 tonnes is the lowest for a year.
Aluminium's recent mini-rally faltered at expected tough resistance around $1,375, and with stocks rising 4,300 tonnes the market retreated to end the session at $1,359, down $10.
Zinc hardly moved throughout the day, ending at $1,019, up just $1 a tonne. Bougrine's suspension again had little impact, although annual capacity is higher at 40,000 tonnes.
But operations are being suspended because zinc prices are low and there appears to be little prospect of serious advances either, analysts noted.

The nickel market was unexciting throughout the session, with business restricted to a tight, generally lower, range. Prices were on the defensive under $7,100 after a 546-tonne stock increase, and last trade was at $7,055, a $25 loss.
Tin edged away from its floor, but there were few features in a slow market, and last trade was at $5,975, up just $20.
Alloy was quoted at a slightly softer $1,230/35 a tonne after scattered trades throughout the day.
